formulas.text: SP = CP × (1 + p) for a profit p, SP = CP × (1 − l) for a loss l.   Profit % = (SP ÷ CP − 1) × 100
formulas.note: Always find the multiplier SP ÷ CP first. 1.144 means 14.4% profit; 0.93 means 7% loss.

formulas.text: MP = CP × (1 + m) and SP = MP × (1 − d), so SP = CP × (1 + m)(1 − d)
formulas.note: Chain the multipliers. Never add and subtract the percentages.

formulas.text: Net % = m − d − (m × d) ÷ 100   (markup m %, discount d %)
formulas.note: The same thing as (1 + m)(1 − d) − 1. For 30 and 12: 30 − 12 − 3.6 = 14.4.

formulas.text: Successive discounts d₁ and d₂ together = d₁ + d₂ − (d₁ × d₂) ÷ 100
formulas.note: 20% then 15%: 20 + 15 − 3 = 32%, not 35%. The order does not matter.

formulas.text: A flat discount in ₹: SP = CP × (1 + m)(1 − d) − flat.  With profit p: CP = flat ÷ [(1 + m)(1 − d) − (1 + p)]
formulas.note: Profit % = (chain % − 100 × flat ÷ CP): a bigger CP gives a bigger profit, which helps pick among options.

formulas.text: False weight: the customer pays for the true weight and receives the false weight. Profit % = (true − false) ÷ false × 100
formulas.note: Divide by the false weight (what the dealer really gave), not the true one. 25% short means false = ¾ of true, so profit = ⅓ = 33⅓%.

formulas.text: False weight with markup and discount: multiplier = (1 + m)(1 − d) × true ÷ false.  Profit % = multiplier − 1
formulas.note: 6% discount and a weight 25% short: 0.94 × 4/3 = 1.2533, i.e. 25.33%.

formulas.text: Buy n, get f free: each unit received costs the buyer price × n ÷ (n + f)
formulas.note: 3 free with every 10 means 13 units for the price of 10.

formulas.text: 'n for ₹x' means ₹x ÷ n each. To compare two rates, use the LCM of the two quantities so that both are whole numbers
formulas.note: 5 for ₹40 is ₹8 each. Selling 4 for ₹10 against buying 3 for ₹10: take 12 articles, cost ₹40, sale ₹30.

formulas.text: Goods mixed in the ratio a : b : c cost (a·c₁ + b·c₂ + c·c₃) ÷ (a + b + c) per unit
formulas.note: The cost of the mix always lies between the cheapest and the dearest component. That alone decides profit or loss in many questions.

formulas.text: Profit at SP₁ equals loss at SP₂ ⇒ CP = (SP₁ + SP₂) ÷ 2.   Profit % at SP₁ = (SP₁ − SP₂) ÷ (SP₁ + SP₂) × 100
formulas.note: Selling at the midpoint of the two prices is selling at cost: no profit, no loss.

formulas.text: Two articles sold at the same price, one at x % profit and one at x % loss ⇒ net loss of x² ÷ 100 % of the total cost
formulas.note: 20% and 20% gives a 4% loss. It is never a gain and never zero.

formulas.text: Overall profit % = (total money received − total cost) ÷ total cost × 100
formulas.note: Add up what came in and what went out first, then compare. Donated units bring nothing in; free units bring nothing in either.

formulas.text: Cost of n articles = selling price of m articles ⇒ profit % = (n − m) ÷ m × 100  (a loss if n is smaller than m)
formulas.note: Divide by the number on the SELLING side. SP of 8 = CP of 10 gives 2/8 = 25% profit; SP of 15 = CP of 10 gives a loss of 5/15 = 33⅓%.

formulas.text: CP : SP = a : b ⇒ profit % = (b − a) ÷ a × 100  (loss % = (a − b) ÷ a × 100)
formulas.note: Put the cost at 100 (or at a) and read the profit off the difference. CP is 80% of SP means CP : SP = 4 : 5, a profit of 25%.

formulas.text: A swing of ₹d between two selling prices that give profits p₁ and p₂ ⇒ CP = d ÷ (p₂ − p₁)  (a loss counts as a negative profit)
formulas.note: A loss of 20% becoming a gain of 15% is a swing of 35% of the cost. If ₹70 caused it, CP = 70 ÷ 0.35 = ₹200.

formulas.text: Profit on N articles equals the selling price of n of them ⇒ profit % = n ÷ (N − n) × 100.  If it equals the cost of n: profit % = n ÷ N × 100
formulas.note: Profit on 20 = SP of 5: 5 ÷ 15 = 33⅓%. The same relation with a loss gives loss % = n ÷ (N + n) × 100 when the loss equals the SP of n.

formulas.text: Parts of a stock sold at different rates: total profit = sum of (part × rate); overall % = total profit ÷ total cost × 100
formulas.note: Use the cost of each part as its weight. A loss part subtracts. Never average the rates unless the parts have the same cost.

formulas.text: Profit of p % on the SELLING price ⇒ CP = SP × (100 − p) ÷ 100, and profit on cost = p ÷ (100 − p) × 100
formulas.note: 20% on selling price is 25% on cost. 10% on selling price turns a cost of ₹27 into SP = 27 ÷ 0.9 = ₹30.

formulas.text: If the price rises p %, spending stays the same when consumption falls by p ÷ (100 + p) × 100 %.  If it falls p %, consumption can rise by p ÷ (100 − p) × 100 %
formulas.note: A 20% rise needs a 16⅔% cut in use. Spend = price × quantity, so the two change in opposite ratios.

formulas.text: MP = SP ÷ (1 − d).   Discount % = (MP − SP) ÷ MP × 100.   A discount is always on the marked price; a profit is always on the cost
formulas.note: Sold at 86% of the marked price: MP = SP ÷ 0.86. A second discount is taken on the price already reduced, so the second rate = 1 − final ÷ (price after the first).

formulas.text: True discount = A × r × t ÷ (100 + r × t);  Banker's discount = A × r × t ÷ 100  (A the sum due, r % a year, t years)
formulas.note: True discount is interest on the present worth; banker's discount is interest on the sum due, so BD = TD × (1 + rt/100). A sum due in 2 years at 5% has TD = A × 10/110.

formulas.text: Earnings = commission % × all sales + bonus % × (sales over the limit)
formulas.note: Write earnings as one rate on total sales minus a fixed amount: 5½% on all plus ½% over 10,000 is 6% of S − 50.

q-pl-chain.cue: A marked price above cost, one or more discounts (maybe a flat ₹ off), then the profit % or the cost price is asked.
q-pl-chain.standard: Call the cost 100 (or CP). Marked price = CP × (1 + m). Selling price = marked price × (1 − d). Profit % = SP ÷ CP − 1. If the SP is given and the CP asked, divide the SP by the chain multiplier.
q-pl-chain.fast: Multiply the decimals once: 1.3 × 0.88 = 1.144, so 14.4%. For two discounts use 0.8 × 0.85 = 0.68 (32% off), never 35%. If the SP is given, CP = SP ÷ multiplier.
q-pl-chain.ultra: Net % = m − d − md ÷ 100: 30 − 12 − 3.6 = 14.4. When the SP is large and the CP is asked, round the multiplier: 1.156 ≈ 1.16, so 39,312 ÷ 1.16 ≈ 33,900, and pick the nearest option.
q-pl-chain.eliminate: (1) With a discount the net profit is always below the markup, so any option at or above the markup is out. (2) Estimate the multiplier and divide: options far from the result are out. (3) When the equation has a flat ₹ discount, profit grows with CP, so test the biggest and smallest option first.
traps: Adding and subtracting percentages (30 − 12 = 18) instead of chaining them.
Giving the discount amount as a % of cost (12% of 130 = 15.6) instead of the profit.
Adding two successive discounts (20% + 15% = 35%) instead of combining them (32%).
Taking the discount on the cost price instead of the marked price.
Dividing by the multiplier when the question wants you to multiply, and the reverse.
variations: Profit given on the selling price instead of the cost price.
Cost of x articles equals the selling price of y articles.
Discount plus overheads (transport, repairs) added to the cost before the profit.
Find the marked price for a target profit after a given discount.
Two successive discounts equal to one single discount.

q-pl-weight.cue: 'Uses a weight of 900 g for 1 kg', or 'a weight 25% less than the actual', possibly with a markup or discount as well.
q-pl-weight.standard: Say the dealer charges for 1 kg but gives less. Money received for the goods he handed over, divided by what those goods cost him, gives the multiplier. With a discount, multiply by (1 − d) first.
q-pl-weight.fast: 25% less means he hands over ¾ of what he charges for, so multiply by 4/3: 94 × 4 ÷ 3 = 125.33 → 25.33%.
q-pl-weight.ultra: Turn the shortage into a fraction (25% = ¼, so false = ¾ of true), then multiply the 'sold at' percentage by the inverse: 94 × 4 ÷ 3 by hand is 376 ÷ 3.
q-pl-weight.eliminate: When the options are only about 1% apart, estimates cannot separate them, so use the decimal tail: 94 × 4 ÷ 3 ends in .33, and only one option ends that way. Also check the sign: a short weight can only add profit, never remove it.
traps: Dividing by the true weight instead of the false weight (25% short gives 33⅓%, not 25%).
Treating the shortage as the profit itself (25% short is not 25% profit).
Subtracting the discount from the gain: 33⅓ − 6 = 27⅓ is wrong; the effects multiply.
Ignoring the markup when one is given.
variations: A weight that is x grams short per kg, with no discount (pure gain).
Dishonest dealer who also claims to sell at cost price.
False weight with a markup and a discount together.
Cheating both ways: buys with a heavier weight and sells with a lighter one.

q-pl-free.cue: 'Buy 3 get 1 free', units donated or given away, and the overall profit or loss on the whole lot.
q-pl-free.standard: Work out the cost of everything, then the money that came in: units sold × price after discount, spread over the free units (money = units handed out × price × n ÷ (n + f)). Overall % = (money in − cost) ÷ cost.
q-pl-free.ultra: Sign first. Even with no free units the receipts (1,200 × 93.5 = ₹1,12,200) are below the cost (₹1,20,000), so it is a loss. The free units can only make it worse.
q-pl-free.eliminate: (1) Sign check: if the best case already loses money, every 'profit' option is out. (2) The free units cut the receipts by 3/13 (about 23%), so the loss must be well above the no-free-units loss of 6.5%.
traps: Counting all the units as sold, including the donated ones.
Forgetting the free units (gives a 6.5% loss instead of 28.08%).
Treating '3 free with 10' as 30% off instead of 13 units for the price of 10.
Using the marked price instead of the discounted price.
variations: Buy 3 get 1 free with a further percentage discount.
Some units spoil or are given away before the sale.
A bulk discount on the whole order and free units on top.
Overall profit when only part of the stock is sold at a loss.

q-pl-rate.cue: Prices given as 'n for ₹x', or several kinds of goods mixed in a ratio and sold at one rate.
q-pl-rate.standard: Find the cost per piece of each kind (x ÷ n). Mix in the given ratio to get the cost per piece of the mix. Find the selling price per piece. Profit % = SP ÷ CP − 1.
q-pl-rate.fast: Costs ₹8, ₹7.50, ₹9 per piece; mix 2 : 2 : 3 costs (16 + 15 + 27) ÷ 7 = 58/7. Selling price 32/3. Multiply both by 21: cost 174, sale 224, so 50/174 ≈ 28.7%.
q-pl-rate.ultra: Multiply both prices by the LCM of the denominators (7 and 3 give 21) so no fraction appears: 174 and 224.
q-pl-rate.eliminate: (1) Sign check: if the selling price per piece is above every cost per piece, it is a profit, and every loss option is out. (2) The mix cost lies between the cheapest and the dearest; use it to bound the profit %.
traps: Using the simple average of the costs instead of the weighted one.
Reading 'n for ₹x' upside down (5 for ₹40 is ₹8 each, not ₹0.125).
Comparing a price for one count with a price for another count without a common unit.
variations: Same quantity bought at two rates and the whole lot sold at a third rate.
Two kinds of grain mixed in a ratio and sold at a given rate.
Buys at n for ₹x and sells at m for ₹y; find the profit %.
Find the selling rate for a target profit.

q-pl-equal.cue: 'Profit at one price equals the loss at another', or two articles sold at the same price with equal % profit and loss.
q-pl-equal.standard: Profit at SP₁ is SP₁ − CP; loss at SP₂ is CP − SP₂. Set them equal: CP = (SP₁ + SP₂) ÷ 2. Then find the result at any third price from that CP.
q-pl-equal.fast: The cost is the midpoint of the two prices: (2,400 + 2,000) ÷ 2 = 2,200.
q-pl-equal.ultra: Add and halve. If the third price is also the midpoint, the answer is 'no profit, no loss' before you calculate anything.
q-pl-equal.eliminate: Look at the third price first: if it is exactly halfway between the two given prices, only the 'no profit, no loss' option can be right.
traps: Assuming the cost equals one of the two selling prices.
Finding the profit % on the selling price instead of the cost.
Thinking that equal profit % and loss % on two articles cancel each other (they do not: it is a net loss).
variations: Same profit at one price and loss at another, then a target profit %.
Two articles at the same selling price, one at x% profit and one at x% loss.
Profit % at one price is double the loss % at another.

q-pl-basic.cue: Cost, selling price, profit or loss given in rupees or articles, sometimes with overheads, damaged goods or a split of money.
q-pl-basic.standard: Add every cost (price, repairs, transport) to get the true cost. Subtract any goods that cannot be sold when working out what comes in. Then profit % = (money in − cost) ÷ cost × 100.
q-pl-basic.fast: Find the multiplier SP ÷ CP once and read the profit from it. When the answer must be a cost, divide the selling price by (1 ± the rate).
q-pl-basic.eliminate: Check the sign first: if the money in is below the cost it is a loss and every 'profit' option is out. Then test the options against the cost, not against the selling price.
traps: Leaving out the repair or transport cost.
Dividing the profit by the selling price.
Counting damaged goods as sold.
Using the dozen price as if it were the price of one.
variations: Best transaction by percentage profit (compare ratios, not rupees).
Two items with equal profit amounts at different rates.
Cost shared in a ratio and one price given.

q-pl-swap.cue: 'The cost price of 15 articles equals the selling price of 10 articles', or 'sells 8 at the price of 10'.
q-pl-swap.standard: Take the price of one article as 1 on the side given. If the cost of n equals the SP of m, then SP of one = n ÷ m times its cost. Profit % = (n − m) ÷ m × 100.
q-pl-swap.fast: Subtract the two numbers, divide by the number on the selling side: 15 and 10 give 5 ÷ 10 = 50%. Larger number on the cost side means a profit; larger on the selling side means a loss.
q-pl-swap.eliminate: Sign check: the bigger count on the cost side is a profit, otherwise a loss. Then divide by the selling count: options that use the cost count are out.
traps: Dividing by the cost count instead of the selling count (10 and 15 gives 33⅓% instead of 50%).
Reversing profit and loss.
Treating the difference in numbers as the profit % directly.
variations: SP of n articles equals CP of m articles (the same relation read the other way).
Large counts such as 2750 and 2500: cancel the common factor first.
'Sells x at the cost of y' wording.

q-pl-ratio.cue: 'CP : SP is 5 : 6', 'SP is 8/5 of CP', 'CP is 80% of SP', or a profit % asked as a ratio of prices.
q-pl-ratio.standard: Write CP and SP as the numbers of the ratio, or as 100 and the multiplier. Profit % = (SP − CP) ÷ CP × 100. To go the other way, turn the profit % into a multiplier and write the ratio.
q-pl-ratio.fast: 5 : 6 means profit 1 on 5 = 20%. 'CP is 80% of SP' means CP : SP = 4 : 5, a profit of 25%, not 20%.
q-pl-ratio.eliminate: A profit % found on the SP is always smaller than the profit on cost, so any option equal to (SP − CP) ÷ SP is a trap.
traps: Dividing by SP (80% gives 20%, but the profit on cost is 25%).
Reversing the ratio (SP : CP).
Reading 200% profit as SP = 2 × CP (it is 3 × CP).
variations: Ratio of two selling prices that give a profit and a loss.
SP is a multiple of CP.
Profit given, ratio SP : CP asked.

q-pl-reprice.cue: 'Sold at a loss of 10% for ₹240; at what price will he gain 20%?' or 'wanted a profit but sold at a loss'.
q-pl-reprice.standard: Find the cost from the given price (price ÷ multiplier). Then the new price = cost × new multiplier.
q-pl-reprice.fast: Scale directly: new price = given price × new multiplier ÷ old multiplier = 240 × 1.2 ÷ 0.9 = 320.
q-pl-reprice.eliminate: The new price must lie above the given one when the new profit is higher, and below when it is lower. Test only the options on the correct side.
traps: Adding the two percentages to the given price instead of finding the cost first.
Applying the new % to the given price instead of the cost.
variations: Wanted a profit, sold at an equal loss for ₹x: find the intended price.
Two prices give a profit % and a loss %: find the cost.
Selling price for a target profit after an overhead.

q-pl-difference.cue: 'If sold for ₹10 more, he would gain 10% instead of losing 10%', or 'a gain of 5% instead of a loss of 5% gives ₹5 more'.
q-pl-difference.standard: The extra rupees are the swing between the two rates, taken as a percent of the cost. Cost = extra ÷ (swing %).
q-pl-difference.fast: Swing = 10% + 10% = 20% of CP = ₹10, so CP = ₹50. Gain 5% instead of loss 5% is a 10% swing: ₹5 ÷ 0.1 = ₹50.
q-pl-difference.eliminate: Plug each option into the swing: swing % × option must equal the extra rupees. Only one option does.
traps: Using only one of the two rates (loss alone, or gain alone).
Using the extra amount as a percent of the selling price.
variations: Loss becomes gain after a price rise of ₹d.
Both prices given as ₹ values and both profits as %.
Selling price raised by a % instead of ₹.

q-pl-profit-in-articles.cue: 'The profit on 17 balls equals the cost of 5', 'a profit equal to the selling price of 5 books'.
q-pl-profit-in-articles.standard: Write the total profit (or loss) in terms of the cost or price of one article, set it equal to the article count in the statement, and solve for the price. Use total SP − total CP = profit.
q-pl-profit-in-articles.fast: Loss equal to the cost of 5 on 17 balls: the 17 balls sold for the cost of 12, so cost per ball = 720 ÷ 12 = ₹60.
q-pl-profit-in-articles.eliminate: Divide the total selling price by the number of 'effective' articles: the options far from that quotient are out.
traps: Mixing up cost and selling price in the statement.
Using all 17 articles as the base instead of the effective 12.
variations: Profit equal to the selling price of n articles.
Loss equal to the selling price of n articles.
Find the profit % from the statement alone.

q-pl-partial.cue: 'One third at 4, half at 5, the rest at cost', or 'two-thirds sold at 5% profit and the rest at 2% loss, total profit ₹400'.
q-pl-partial.standard: Split the stock into the given parts. Find the profit (or loss) on each part using that part's cost. Add the profits and subtract the losses. Overall % = net ÷ total cost.
q-pl-partial.fast: Take the total cost as 1 (or as a convenient number like 120). Then each part's contribution is part × rate. Two-thirds at +5% and one-third at −2% gives 10/3 − 2/3 = 8/3 = 2.667% of the whole.
q-pl-partial.eliminate: The overall % lies between the smallest and the largest of the part rates. Options outside that band are out.
traps: Averaging the rates without weighting by the part sizes.
Treating the loss part as a profit.
Weighting by selling price instead of cost.
variations: Part of the stock goes bad before sale.
Overall profit given; find the total value or one part's rate.
Three or more parts with the rest sold at cost.

q-pl-profit-on-sp.cue: 'Profit of 10% on the selling price', 'cost is 13/15 of the selling price'.
q-pl-profit-on-sp.standard: Convert to cost basis: if the profit is p % of SP, then CP = SP × (100 − p) ÷ 100 and profit on cost = p ÷ (100 − p) × 100. Then solve as a normal profit question.
q-pl-profit-on-sp.fast: 10% on SP means CP is 90% of SP, so SP = 27 ÷ 0.9 = ₹30.
q-pl-profit-on-sp.eliminate: Profit quoted on SP is smaller than the same figure on cost, so a profit on cost of 10% gives a smaller price than a profit on SP of 10%: use that to reject the wrong pair.
traps: Treating the 10% as a profit on cost (27 × 1.1 = 29.70).
Using 110% instead of 90% for the SP.
variations: Cost given as a fraction of SP.
Profit on SP converted to profit on cost.
Two selling prices, one quoted on cost and one on SP.

q-pl-sellers.cue: 'A sells to B at a profit of 10%, B sells to C at a loss of 10%', 'C paid ₹91', or a jewel passing through three hands.
q-pl-sellers.standard: Each seller's selling price is the next seller's cost. Multiply the multipliers in order: price paid by C = A's cost × m₁ × m₂. Divide to go backwards.
q-pl-sellers.fast: 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99: the first seller ends up 1% better off than the starting price. Use the product, not the sum, of the percentages.
q-pl-sellers.eliminate: Equal profit and loss in a chain never cancel: 10% up then 10% down leaves a 1% drop. Any 'no change' option is out unless the multipliers cancel exactly.
traps: Adding and subtracting the percentages (10% − 10% = 0).
Applying the second % to the original cost instead of to the new price.
Dividing when the chain asks you to multiply.
variations: Goods rising 65% over three hands with two known profits.
Buy-back at a loss.
Final price given; find the first cost.

q-pl-successive.cue: 'Successive discounts of 10%, 20% and 25%', or 'find the single discount equivalent to…'.
q-pl-successive.standard: Convert each discount into a multiplier (90% = 0.9) and multiply: 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.75 = 0.54, so the single discount is 46%.
q-pl-successive.fast: For two discounts: d₁ + d₂ − d₁d₂ ÷ 100. For three, do the first two, then combine that with the third.
q-pl-successive.eliminate: The combined discount is always less than the sum of the discounts and more than the largest one. Both bounds remove options.
traps: Adding the discounts (10 + 20 + 25 = 55%).
Taking the second discount on the original price instead of the reduced price.
Using the rate as a multiplier instead of (1 − rate).
variations: Discount on a bundle given the price of three.
A discount then a free item.
Equivalent single discount given and one unknown.

q-pl-quantity.cue: 'A 20% fall in the price lets him buy 4 kg more for ₹100', 'salary reduced by 10%: how much must it rise to return?'.
q-pl-quantity.standard: Spend = price × quantity. Write the price change as a multiplier, the quantity change as its inverse, and equate the spend. Solve for the unknown rate or the percent.
q-pl-quantity.fast: A fall of p % in price lets you buy p ÷ (100 − p) more: 20% fall lets you buy 25% more. To undo a 10% cut you need 10 ÷ 90 = 11⅑%.
q-pl-quantity.eliminate: The rise needed to undo a fall of p % is always bigger than p %; the cut needed to offset a rise of p % is always smaller. Both remove options.
traps: Using the same percent both ways (a 10% cut is not undone by a 10% rise).
Applying the new price to the old quantity.
variations: Consumption cut needed to keep spending the same after a rise.
Price falls and the extra quantity is given in kg.
Salary or income cut and restored.

q-pl-marked.cue: 'What price should he mark to gain 20% after a 10% discount?', 'sold at ₹387 after 14% off: the marked price?', 'a discount saves ₹150: the marked price?'.
q-pl-marked.standard: Find the selling price needed (cost × (1 + profit)) or the price paid. Then marked price = selling price ÷ (1 − discount).
q-pl-marked.fast: One line: cost × 1.2 ÷ 0.9. If a saving is given, the marked price is the saving ÷ the discount rate.
q-pl-marked.eliminate: The marked price is always above the selling price and above the cost. Options below either are out, and so is the selling price itself.
traps: Stopping at the selling price (cost × 1.2) and calling it the marked price.
Multiplying by 1.1 instead of dividing by 0.9.
Adding the profit and the discount percentages.
variations: Percent above cost to mark the goods.
A second (cash) discount on top of the first.
Sales tax added after the discount.
A saving equal to the price of another article.

q-pl-discount-rate.cue: 'Find the rate of discount', 'the second discount', 'what additional discount brings the price to ₹1,104?'.
q-pl-discount-rate.standard: Discount % = (marked − selling) ÷ marked × 100. For a second discount, first find the price after the first, then take the second on that price. When a profit is given, the selling price is cost × (1 + profit).
q-pl-discount-rate.fast: Final ÷ price after the first discount, then 1 − that: 550.80 ÷ 648 = 0.85, so 15%.
q-pl-discount-rate.eliminate: The extra discount, taken on the reduced price, is always larger than it would be on the list price: options equal to (list − final) ÷ list are traps.
traps: Dividing the saving by the selling price instead of the marked price.
Subtracting the first discount from the total saving percent.
Taking the second discount on the list price.
variations: Equal discounts compared on two articles (ratio of costs).
Buy 4 get 1 free (1/5 = 20%).
Mark above cost, then a discount for a target profit.
Discount on a bundle of several articles.

q-pl-commission.cue: '5½% commission on all sales plus ½% bonus on sales over ₹10,000', or 'total commission ₹56,100 and one gets 12% more than the other'.
q-pl-commission.standard: Write the earnings as a rate on all the sales and a rate on the part above the limit. Combine into one equation and solve for the sales.
q-pl-commission.fast: Merge the rates: 6% of S minus 50 = 1,990, so S = 2,040 ÷ 0.06 = 34,000.
q-pl-commission.eliminate: Test each option: 6% of the option minus the bonus adjustment must give the earnings.
traps: Applying the bonus to all sales instead of the part over the limit.
Splitting the total in the ratio 12 : 100 instead of 112 : 100.
variations: Two people whose commissions differ by a percent.
Commission slabs with different rates.
Salary plus commission.

q-pl-true-discount.cue: 'True discount on a sum due 2 years hence at 5%', 'banker's discount on a bill due 6 months hence'.
q-pl-true-discount.standard: True discount = sum × rt ÷ (100 + rt). Banker's discount = sum × rt ÷ 100. Convert the time to years first.
q-pl-true-discount.fast: TD ÷ sum = rt ÷ (100 + rt): at 5% for 2 years it is 10/110, so sum = 11 × TD. BD ÷ TD = 1 + rt/100.
q-pl-true-discount.eliminate: Banker's discount is always larger than the true discount; the true discount is always smaller than the sum.
traps: Using the sum due as if it were the present worth.
Forgetting to convert 6 months to ½ year.
variations: Find the time from the TD and sum.
Find BD from TD, or TD from BD.
Find the rate.

pyqs.text: A company made 1,500 units at a total cost of ₹1,20,000 and donated 300 units to an NGO. The rest was sold at a 15% discount on the market price of ₹110 a unit, with 3 units free for every 10 bought. If all 1,500 units were distributed, what is the overall gain or loss %?

3 free with every 10 bought: buyers get 13 units for 10 paid, so only 1,200 × 10/13 ≈ 923.08 units are paid for.
